items: Static membership: set `group.instance.id`.
A short restart within `session.timeout.ms` triggers none.
Manual `assign()` pins partitions, no group, no failover.

blocks.title: Classic Bug
blocks.text: Slow per-record work exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer is evicted mid-batch, the work is reprocessed, and lag grows further.

items: Auto-commit: at-most or at-least-once, depends on failure point.
`commitSync()` after processing: at-least-once.
Exactly-once needs a transactional producer.
Set `transactional.id` plus `isolation.level=read_committed`.

blocks.title: The Health Metric
blocks.text: Consumer lag per partition = end offset minus committed offset. Watch MAX lag across partitions, never the average.

items: `delete` drops whole segments past retention.ms/bytes.
`compact` turns the log into a changelog or table.
`compact,delete` suits Streams changelogs with bounded history.

blocks.title: Why Partition Count Is Frozen
blocks.text: Compaction is per-partition and keyed. Changing the count splits one key's history across two partitions and corrupts the table view.

blocks.title: Common Mistake
blocks.text: Sizing disk with retention.bytes read as a topic total, then filling the disk twelve times over.

items: Compaction runs per partition, independently.
It never touches the active segment.
So the newest records are always uncompacted.
`min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` default 0.5 gates the work.
Time retention keys off the record timestamp.
A backfill with old create-times can be deleted on arrival.
`segment.bytes` and `segment.ms` set deletion granularity.
Huge segments delay reclaiming space.

blocks.title: Tiered Storage (KIP-405)
items: Cold segments move to object storage.
Partition retention exceeds local disk.
Replay is slower but far cheaper.

blocks.title: Reprocessing Limit
blocks.text: `seekToBeginning()` only replays what retention still holds on disk. Beginning means oldest surviving offset, not offset zero.

items: Hot key: one partition at 90% of traffic, eleven idle.
Check per-partition byte rate, never the topic rate.
Null keys where order mattered: sticky scattered a user.
That user's events lost their sequence permanently.

blocks.title: The Destructive Alter
blocks.text: Increasing partitions on a live keyed topic: the same key now hashes elsewhere, so ordering and compaction history both break.
With in-flight > 1 and no idempotence, a retried batch lands after a later batch and the partition order is gone.

slides.page_title: Ordering Pitfalls, Monitoring & The Four Rules

blocks.title: Pick The Reset On Purpose
blocks.text: The default only applies when no committed offset exists. Decide per group whether a first start should replay history or start clean.

lines: // WRONG: pool per record, order gone

items: Too many: slow controller failover, heavy producer memory.
Long rebalances that look like a broker outage.
Too few: consumers cannot scale out at all.
And the fix, adding partitions, is the destructive op above.

blocks.title: Rebalance Storm
blocks.text: max.poll.interval.ms set too low for real processing time: each eviction adds lag, and more lag causes more evictions.

items: Cross-partition order in a join or aggregation.
Correct only if both sides are co-partitioned.
Same key AND same partition count on both sides.
A consumer read is durable forever: retention may delete it.

blocks.title: Monitoring Gaps To Close
items: `UnderReplicatedPartitions`, `OfflinePartitionsCount`.
`IsrShrinksPerSec`.
Max consumer lag, per partition.
Per-partition byte rate for skew.
Ordering: guaranteed per partition. Want it? Give a stable key.
Parallelism: bounded by partition count per group.
Want more consumers? More partitions first.
Keyed placement: `murmur2(key) % numPartitions`.
Unkeyed: sticky batching, partition undefined.
Uptime-first pipeline? min.insync.replicas=1.
Accept possible loss on leader failure, in writing.
Never enable unclean leader election unless availability
strictly outranks correctness, and document that choice.

rows: leader only, loses on leader failure

items: Raising min.insync.replicas always costs write availability.
Lowering it always costs durability. There is no free setting.
Partitions = target throughput / per-partition consumer rate.
Round up for headroom, then live with it for a year.
Key cardinality must be far above partition count.
The entity that needs order must BE the key.
Target 60k records/s, one consumer handles 5k/s.
60k / 5k = 12 partitions, the bare minimum.
Round up to 16 for headroom and growth.
16 partitions at RF=3 = 48 replicas on disk.

blocks.title: Compacted Topic Rule
items: Pick the partition count once.
Never change it.
Always key every record.
retention.bytes is per partition: x parts x RF.

blocks.title: Hot Key Fixes
blocks.text: Composite key (`userId#bucket`), key salting, or a two-stage aggregate. Each one buys throughput and costs strict per-user order.

items: No global order across partitions. Ever, at any config.
Multi-topic order is undefined, always.
Timestamps do not restore order: create time is client-supplied.
Co-partition both sides before any join.

blocks.title: The Whole Handbook, One Line
blocks.text: Kafka gives ordered, replicated, per-partition logs: the key chooses the partition, the partition count caps parallelism, and ISR plus acks decides what "written" really means.

caption.text: Part 2 of KAFKA FIELD NOTES. Kafka does not order your topic. It orders a partition, and your key is what decides which one a record lands in — everything else follows from that. 10 pages of field notes: log mechanics and offsets, murmur2 partitioning, why adding partitions is a one-way destructive door, RF vs ISR vs acks, cooperative rebalancing, compaction rules, and the failure modes that look like durability but aren't. Save it before your next topic design review.
